source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on a text-only Raven-style task (Digit Matrices) with no examples.
numbers: Humans N=40. Generative answers: GPT-3 vs humans odds ratio 1.88, p=0.005, CI [1.21,2.91]. Multiple choice: OR 6.27, p=2.3e-8. The best human got every item right. Item-type pattern correlated with humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: Items were built for the study, so new to the model, but they are text, so no visual parsing was tested. Authors found no sign of memorisation. Result is strongest for the RLHF variant.
agent_relevance: A text-form Gf test can be solved zero-shot by a big model, so unfamiliarity alone does not mark a problem as hard for an LLM. Test the problem form, not just novelty.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 difficulty effects had the same direction as human relational-complexity effects but were larger.
numbers: Progression vs none, odds ratio: humans 0.41 (p=0.0001), GPT-3 0.07. Number of unique rules: humans 0.61, GPT-3 0.25. Permuted vs aligned logic items: humans 0.52, GPT-3 0.06. On story analogies students beat GPT-3 (OR 0.37, p=0.0003; 15 of 54 humans perfect); a GPT-4 preview did far better.
limits: Same direction does not mean same process. Only GPT-3 and a GPT-4 preview on one task.
agent_relevance: Counting rules and bindings in a problem gives a cheap code-side difficulty score for the S0 gate.

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual replication of Webb: GPT models drop on letter-string analogies with shuffled or symbol alphabets; humans do not.
numbers: Overall accuracy: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Human accuracy stayed flat across 0, 2, 5, 10, 20 permuted letters; GPT fell at each step and again for symbols.
limits: Prolific humans scored higher than Webb's students. Comprehension checks show GPT-4 knew the new order (mostly 0.9 to 1.0), so the failure is in applying it. Newest reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Success on familiar-looking items may reflect memorised form. Use an altered-surface twin as a held-out check (G3).

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Partial failed replication: on the unaltered problems the GPT models did not beat humans as Webb reported, and item-type results differed.
numbers: Authors' GPT-3 overall was close to Webb's but differed on Predecessor and Fix Alphabet; GPT-3.5 differed on Remove Redundant, Fix Alphabet, Sort; GPT-4 on Remove Redundant and Sort. GPT runs used the Hodel and West (2023) prompt.
limits: Cost limited samples. Prompt wording moved scores. Human pool differed.
agent_relevance: Scores on Gf-like items depend on prompt format. Fix one format and log it when sorting items by novelty.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: On open-ended abstract reasoning (ARC, Raven-style, PVR, BIG-Bench-F, Evals-S) LLMs failed most items; GPT-4 was best.
numbers: Open QA accuracy, GPT-4: ARC 0.119, BIG-Bench-F 0.514, Evals-S 0.304, PVR 0.177, Raven text 0.410, Raven symbolic 0.330. Davinci-3: ARC 0.105, Raven text 0.343. GPT-3.5-turbo: ARC 0.033, Raven text 0.226. LLaMA-7B near 0 on most.
limits: 2023 models. Raven items generated by the authors. They suspect GPT-4 saw Raven-type tests in training, since its gain is largest there.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of 2023 models was weak on rule induction from few examples. Flag that class of problem.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Prompting and refinement methods that help ordinary NLP tasks did not help abstract reasoning; the bottleneck is spotting unseen patterns.
numbers: More in-context examples helped only Davinci-3 and GPT-4 on BIG-Bench-F (up to 0.6 at 16 examples) and not on PVR (Davinci-3 0.26 at 12 examples). Chain-of-thought and code refinement gave small or negative changes.
limits: BIG-Bench-F gains likely reflect list-processing seen in training. No reasoning-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume chain-of-thought alone fixes failure on novel rules; real checks are needed (G2, G3).

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Fine-tuning on Raven-style data gave near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fell on compositional out-of-distribution splits.
numbers: LLaMA2 fine-tuned on symbolic RAVEN reached 96.5% on the text task; accuracy dropped significantly on the -Four and -In-Center splits. Base LLaMA stayed near 0.
limits: Small open models only.
agent_relevance: Skill from many items does not carry to new compositions, so novel compositions need a different route than familiar ones.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Input format moderates results: on causal-induction tasks (ACRE) GPT models overfit backward-blocking cases in text but not in symbolic form.
numbers: Open Raven QA GPT-4: text 0.410, symbolic 0.330 (text higher). GPT-3.5-turbo text 0.226, symbolic 0.161.
limits: Direction differs between ACRE and Raven, so format effects are task dependent.
agent_relevance: Normalise problem encoding before rule induction, and log the format.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: ConceptARC tests 16 spatial concepts in easy variants; people score near ceiling, programs and GPT-4 do not.
numbers: 480 tasks. Humans over 90% on 11 of 16 concepts and over 80% on the rest; overall 91%. Kaggle first place 52% (below 60% on 11 of 16 concepts); second place below 50% on 15 of 16; GPT-4 25% overall, below 30% on 15 of 16 concepts. 482 human participants, 12 excluded by attention checks.
limits: Mechanical Turk and Prolific samples. GPT-4 text version, zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Easy variants for people can still defeat machines, so surface novelty and real difficulty differ.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: Richer one-shot prompts helped GPT-4 a little; multimodal GPT-4V did worse than text-only GPT-4.
numbers: ConceptARC overall: GPT-4 one-shot 0.33 at both temperatures vs earlier zero-shot 0.19 (temp 0) and 0.25 (temp 0.5). Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 text 0.69 (temp 0), 0.65 (temp 0.5), GPT-4V zero-shot 0.25, one-shot 0.23.
limits: GPT-4V run only on the simplest tasks for cost. Image reading was inconsistent.
agent_relevance: An example in the prompt added 8 to 14 points but a large gap remained. Input format can matter more than size.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
finding: ARC-AGI-1 private score rose from 33% to 55.5% in 2024, driven by test-time training and program-search ensembles.
numbers: Kaggle winner ARChitects 53.5% (open); MindsAI 55.5% (closed); 2020 top 20%. Semi-private/public: Berman 53.6%/58.5%, Akyurek et al. 47.5%/62.8%, Greenblatt 43%/42%, o1-preview 18%/21%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14%/21%, GPT-4o 5%/9%. $600,000 grand prize (85%) unclaimed.
limits: Kaggle entries had about $10 of compute; ARC-AGI-Pub up to $10,000 of API credits. Public-vs-semi-private gap up to 15 points (Akyurek) shows overfitting risk.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of frontier models scored 5 to 21%; systems that adapt at test time scored far higher.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
finding: Two solver families (induction by program, transduction by direct prediction) fail on different items; only an ensemble competes.
numbers: Induction-only and transduction-only single submissions each score around 40%; static transduction without test-time training stays under 11%. In 2020 the best single entry scored 20% (brute-force program search) but 49% of the private set was solved by at least one team.
limits: Static benchmark; brute force and leakage inflate scores.
agent_relevance: Different solvers cover different items. Selection or agreement checks in code beat trusting one solver (G4, G5).

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
finding: Human baseline for ARC is small and informal.
numbers: Original private tasks tested by two people who scored 97% and 98% (together 100%). NYU study: 99% of public evaluation tasks solved by at least one of 10 Mechanical Turk workers.
limits: No standard protocol; the report itself says participant pools, motivation and time limits vary.
agent_relevance: Treat 'humans solve it' as a rough ceiling, not a norm.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A new challenge for frontier AI reasoning systems
finding: ARC-AGI-2 was built harder for AI yet solvable by people; frontier models fell to low single digits.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 vs ARC-AGI-2 semi-private: o3-mini-high 34.5% vs 3.0%; o3-medium 53.0% vs 3.0%; ARChitects 56.0% vs 2.5%; o4-mini 41.8% vs 2.4%; o1-pro 23.3% vs 0.9%; Claude 3.7 (8K) 21.2% vs 0.9%; Icecuber 17.0% vs 1.6%.
limits: Paper says consistent signal appears only above 5%. Snapshot of May 14, 2025.
agent_relevance: Strong scores on one novel set did not carry to a harder one; discount confidence on novel-looking items.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A new challenge for frontier AI reasoning systems
finding: Human calibration for ARC-AGI-2.
numbers: 407 participants, 515 sessions, 13,405 test-pair attempts, 62% solved; median 2.3 min per attempt. Retained tasks were each solved by at least two independent non-experts; 75% of attempts per task and 66% of test pairs succeeded overall.
limits: Paid participants, not a psychometric norm sample. Selection requires human solvability.
agent_relevance: Good rule for novelty items: solvable from the stated examples alone, no outside knowledge.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A new challenge for frontier AI reasoning systems
finding: Compute buys accuracy on novel items: o3 on ARC-AGI-1 scored 76% and 88% at very high cost, and a medium setting scored 53%.
numbers: o3 low compute 76% (about $200 per task), high compute 88% (about $20,000 per task) in the preview run; o3-medium 53% on the semi-private set. Paper states high-end humans solve over 97% of ARC-AGI-1 without much effort, so it saturated below human fluid range.
limits: The preview configuration differs from the released model, per the report.
agent_relevance: Scale samples and search with detected novelty rather than giving all problems the same budget.

source: Akyurek et al. (2025) The surprising effectiveness of test-time training for few-shot learning
finding: Test-time training (a short weight update on the task examples) lifted ARC accuracy sharply.
numbers: 80-task ARC validation subset, pass@2: fine-tuned 17.5% to 45.0% with TTT (+27.5 points). 8B model 53.0% on the public validation set; 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis. BIG-Bench Hard 10-shot 50.5% to 57.8% (+7.3).
limits: Needs weight updates, unavailable to a scaffold-only agent. Public validation set, not private.
agent_relevance: In-context examples under-use available information on novel tasks; a scaffold can re-ask on augmented views and vote in code, but cannot update weights.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) MARVEL: multidimensional abstraction and reasoning through visual evaluation and learning
finding: Multimodal models were near chance on varied abstract visual puzzles and could not reliably perceive the figures.
numbers: 770 puzzles, six patterns, five layouts, nine models. Human accuracy 68.86% (SD 9.74). All models near random on the main question, gap to humans about 40 points. Panel counting below 45%.
limits: Models of early 2024, zero- and few-shot.
agent_relevance: On image inputs check perception first, since reasoning over misread figures is moot.

source: Ilic, Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models
finding: Across 591 LLMs and 12 benchmarks scores correlate positively and form a general factor, like human g.
numbers: Mean inter-test correlation 0.73 (range 0.35 to 0.99). Mean g loading 0.81; g explains 65.6% of variance. Parameter count vs general-factor score: Pearson r=0.54 [0.48,0.59], Spearman 0.62, with diminishing returns. Another factor score vs parameters: Pearson 0.11 [0.05,0.18], Spearman 0.42.
limits: Gf proxies were Hellaswag, GSM8K-style and elementary maths: knowledge-heavy. Authors say it may be achievement, not intelligence.
agent_relevance: Standard benchmark 'Gf' mostly tracks general model strength, so a novelty sort needs genuinely new items.

source: Chollet (2019) On the measure of intelligence
finding: Chollet links CHC fluid versus crystallized intelligence to skill-acquisition efficiency versus stored skill, and proposes ARC to test the former.
numbers: Position paper with no human norm data for ARC.
limits: Theory, not an experiment. Later reports show it measures something models can partly gain with search and training.
agent_relevance: Supports sorting problems by dependence on stored knowledge versus new rule induction.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Working memory training raised working memory scores but not nonverbal reasoning (Raven-type) against active controls.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 comparisons. Nonverbal ability vs treated controls g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13], k=67; vs untreated controls g=0.20 [0.11,0.28], k=53. Verbal working memory g=0.31 (treated), 0.42 (untreated). Criterion task g=0.80 vs 1.88.
limits: The passive-control gain shrinks with active controls, which points to expectation or practice effects. Improvement on working memory did not predict far-transfer size. p-curve analysis found no evidential value for treated-control studies.
agent_relevance: Gf is not raised by drilling its supposed substrate (see subfield 03). Change the process, not the buffer.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: The original far-transfer claim (Raven gains after training) rests on weakly controlled studies.
numbers: Reading comprehension vs treated controls g=0.15 but fell to 0.08 once studies where controls declined were removed. Arithmetic vs treated controls g=0.06.
limits: Pre-test post-test designs only. Age and dose moderators did not rescue transfer.
agent_relevance: Use active comparison arms when we test scaffold changes.

source: Trahan et al. (2014) The Flynn effect: a meta-analysis
finding: IQ scores rose about 3 points a decade and the rise is mostly in fluid-type tests such as Raven's.
numbers: 285 studies, N=14,031 since 1951: mean 2.31 points per decade [1.99,2.64]. Modern Stanford-Binet and Wechsler: 2.93 [2.3,3.5], 53 comparisons, N=3,951. No sign of fading. Sample type and administration order mattered; age and ability level did not.
limits: Atypical pre-1972 samples inflate estimates. Scores rise with more familiarity with test types.
agent_relevance: Gf scores respond to environment and exposure, supporting routing of familiar problem types to known methods.

source: Ritchie, Tucker-Drob (2018) How much does education improve intelligence? A meta-analysis
finding: Schooling raises cognitive test scores; durable gains come from long education, not short drills.
numbers: 142 effect sizes, 42 data sets, over 600,000 participants: about 1 to 5 IQ points per extra year of education; effects persist across the life span and across broad ability categories.
limits: Abstract only was read. Quasi-experimental designs.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot copy schooling, but it can load method knowledge into context.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: The same programs scored much higher on ConceptARC than on the original ARC hidden set, so difficulty depends on task design.
numbers: Original ARC hidden set: Kaggle first and second place solved 21% and 19%; their ensemble about 31%. On ConceptARC the first-place program scored 52% overall.
limits: Different task sets and sizes (100 hidden tasks vs 480 simple tasks).
agent_relevance: Difficulty for a solver is a property of task design, not of the 'Gf' label. Measure per-item, not per-benchmark.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: Authors note GPT-4 did well on other idealised analogy domains (Webb) but poorly on ConceptARC, a boundary on the emergent-analogy claim.
numbers: GPT-4 below 30% on 15 of 16 ConceptARC concepts, one concept 33%.
limits: Zero-shot text prompts; the one-shot follow-up by Mitchell et al. raised GPT-4 to 0.33 overall.
agent_relevance: Analogy success in one format does not predict success in another; sort by format and rule type at S0.
